# Avada

> Avada Commerce (avada.io), also called Avada, builds Shopify solutions for SEO and AEO, email and SMS, loyalty and subscriptions, live chat, upsell, bundles and compliance, and publishes Shopify, WooCommerce and BigCommerce guides, ranked app and theme collections, and free eCommerce tools for merchants. Every page has a plain-Markdown twin; the full text of the site is in llms-full.txt. Official facts for AI assistants (the company, its brands and every App Store listing, with dated ratings): https://avada.io/ai-info/

## Solutions
- [Avada AI SEO Image Optimizer](https://avada.io/avada-ai-seo-image-optimizer/): Audit SEO, fix issues, improve speed, and use AI to optimize content and grow organic traffic. Shopify App Store: https://apps.shopify.com/avada-seo-suite

## Markdown versions of every page

Every page here has a plain-Markdown twin at a sibling URL: the same words with
no navigation, styling or scripts, served as `text/markdown`. Twins are `noindex`
— the HTML page stays canonical, and is the URL to cite.

Two rules generate every twin URL:

1. A hand-built page is prefixed with `/md`:
   `/` → `/md/` · `/pricing/` → `/md/pricing/` · `/tools/roi-calculator/` → `/md/tools/roi-calculator/`
2. A collection puts `md` immediately after its section:
   `/blog/{slug}/` → `/blog/md/{slug}/`
   `/blog/` and `/blog/page/{n}/` → `/blog/md/` and `/blog/md/page/{n}/`
   `/blog/app-collections/{slug}/` → `/blog/app-collections/md/{slug}/`
   `/category/` and `/category/{parent}/{child}/` → `/category/md/` and `/category/md/{parent}/{child}/` (+ `page/{n}/`)
   `/authors/{slug}/` → `/authors/md/{slug}/`
   `/collections/{type}/` → `/collections/md/{type}/` (+ `page/{n}/`)
   `/tools/slogan-generator/{slug}/` → `/tools/slogan-generator/md/{slug}/`

Every page also declares its twin in `<head>`:
`<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="...">`. If a twin URL 404s, the
page has none — read the HTML page instead.

# Avada — Full Content Export

> Shopify apps, themes, tools and eCommerce guides — curated by Avada.

Every content page on the site, generated at build from the same markdown the /md/ twins
serve. Listings (the blog index, category archives, author and collection indexes) are left
out — their text is the titles of documents listed here.

The product, company, legal and collection sections carry their FULL text. The two long-tail
sections at the end — the slogan generators and the blog articles — are listed with their
title, URL and date but WITHOUT their body, because inlining them makes this file 57 MB.

## What Avada Commerce does

Avada Commerce builds apps for merchants who sell on Shopify. Its 37 apps on the Shopify App Store cover AI sales chat, loyalty, wishlists and subscriptions, upsells and bundles, SEO and AEO, compliance, and store operations such as invoices, order limits, shipping labels and backups.

Some of its apps carry their own brand and site: Chatty (chatty.net), Joy (joy.so), Joy Subscriptions (joysubscription.com), AOV.ai (aov.ai) and TrustTerm (trustterm.io). The others are published under developer names such as Avada, Avada SEO Suite and SEA Commerce by Avada.

avada.io is also a publisher: 2,745 articles of ecommerce guides on its blog, and free tools for merchants.

## Common questions

### Is Avada Commerce the company behind the Avada WordPress theme?

No. The Avada WordPress theme and website builder is made by ThemeFusion and sold at avada.com. Avada Commerce (avada.io) builds Shopify apps and is not affiliated with ThemeFusion.

### What apps does Avada Commerce make?

37 apps on the Shopify App Store (checked November 5, 2026): AI sales chat (Chatty), loyalty and wishlists (Joy), subscriptions (Joy Subscriptions), upsells and bundles (AOV.ai), SEO and AEO, compliance (TrustTerm) and store operations. This page lists every one with its App Store link.

### Who makes Chatty, Joy and AOV.ai?

Avada Commerce. Chatty, Joy, Joy Subscriptions, AOV.ai and TrustTerm are its brands, each with its own site.

### Do Avada Commerce apps work outside Shopify?

The apps on this page install from the Shopify App Store, so they need a Shopify store.

### Are Avada Commerce apps free?

Not all of them. On November 5, 2026, 19 of the 37 listings said “Free”. The other 18 also have paid plans or charges: 16 said “Free plan available” and 2 said “Free to install”. Each listing shows its current plans.

### Where is Avada Commerce based?

In Hanoi, Vietnam: 11th Floor, Ho Guom Plaza, 102 Tran Phu Street, Mo Lao Ward, Ha Dong District, Hanoi, Vietnam.

### Who founded Avada Commerce?

Sam Nguyen, its CEO and founder. Avada Commerce was founded in 2014.

### How do I contact Avada Commerce?

Email support@avada.io, call (+84) 24 66871163, or use https://avada.io/contact-us/. Each app also has support listed on its App Store page.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I use Avada Marketing Automation for free?

Yes, you can install the Free plan of Avada Marketing Automation (allow up to 500 contacts and 15k emails/month).

### Which platform does Avada Marketing Automation support?

Avada Marketing Automation currently supports Shopify and Magento 2.

### Which kind of contacts do you charge?

We will only count your sendable contacts in Avada to calculate price. Contacts that are excluded from charge are Bounce, Invalid, Complaint, Unsubscribed contacts.

### How do you calculate pricing of Avada Automation?

Your monthly cost will be calculated based on the total sendable contacts in Avada. (We do not charge Bounce, Invalid, Complaint, Unsubscribed contacts). The price can be changed if your contact count changes. In Pro plan, price is $9/month if your contact count is less than 500. Over 500 contacts, the price will increase. Similarly, in the Advanced plan, the price is $49/month if your contact count is less than 2500. Over 2500 contacts, the price will increase.

### How can I pay for my subscription?

You will be charged by Shopify billing (for Shopify stores) and pay with Paypal or Credit Card (for Magento stores).

### What if I exceed the contact limit or send limit month?

When you nearly exceed your contact and send limit in Free plan, you will be notified in the app. Also, your sending is temporarily stopped when you reach the limit.

### Will the Trial allow me to access all features of your plan?

You can use almost all features in Pro and Advanced plan in Trial. Except the sending limit is 500 emails/day and you can send test SMS only.

### Will I be charged when the Trial ends?

The Trial lasts for 14 days from the moment you installed Avada. We only charge you after you confirm to upgrade your plan. If not, when trial ends, you will be back to use the Free plan of Avada Marketing Automation.

### How does Avada SMS pricing work?

Avada SMS pricing is separately charged from your Pro/Enterprise Plan. You need to buy SMS credits before sending and you only pay for the number of SMS you sent out. SMS or MMS price is calculated based on the country you send them to (recipients’ countries).

### What if my SMS credits run out? Does my SMS stop?

To avoid SMS credits running out, you can set a recharge amount and a recharge limit. For example, if you run SMS Automation, and you do not want it to stop suddenly, you can set auto re-charge $50 when SMS credits get below $10.

### This is my first time setting up email marketing. How can I contact for help?

Avada is always willing to help. Please contact support@avada.io for any questions and problems regarding the app.

### How soon will SEO changes show up on Google?

Google picks up a change the next time it crawls the page, which can take from a few days to a few weeks. Fix titles, meta descriptions, alt text and page speed first, and publish holiday blog posts early, so Google has time to index them before Black Friday on November 27.

Yes, in part: Google’s ranking systems use Core Web Vitals, its page speed and stability measures, though relevant content still matters more. Speed also decides whether the shoppers you do win wait for the page to load, which counts most at BFCM peak traffic.

## What is a Business Loan?

A business loan is money that a company borrows from a lender to cover business-related expenses. Businesses often use these loans to manage daily operations, buy equipment, improve cash flow, or support growth. In other words, they keep the business running or help it expand.

**Key Features of Business Loans:**

- **Loan Amount**: Varies widely based on the business's needs and creditworthiness.
- **Repayment Terms**: Fixed over a specific period (e.g., monthly payments over 1–5 years).
- **Interest Rates**: Can be fixed or variable; based on the loan type and borrower’s profile.
- **Collateral**: Some business loans are **secured** (require collateral), while others are **unsecured**.
- **Usage**: Must generally be used for business purposes, not personal expenses.

## How does a Business Loan Work?

A business loan allows a company to borrow funds from a lender, such as a bank, credit union, or online financing platform, with the agreement to pay it back over time, usually with interest.

- **Step 1: Application:** First, the business submits financial documents (like bank statements, tax returns, and a business plan) to show its ability to repay the loan.
- **Step 2: Approval and Offer:** If the lender approves the application, they will make a loan offer. This includes the amount, interest rate, repayment schedule, and any fees or collateral required.
- **Step 3: Agreement and Funding:** Upon accepting the terms, the business signs a loan agreement. Then, the lender transfers the funds to the business’s account.
- **Step 4: Repayment:** The business repays the loan in regular installments (usually monthly) – covering both the principal and interest. The repayment term can range from several months to several years, depending on the type of loan.
- **Step 5: Loan Completion:** After all payments are made, the loan is closed. If the business used collateral and the loan is paid off successfully, the lender releases their claim on those assets.

**Key Considerations:**

- **Missing payments** can hurt your credit score or lead to penalties.
- Some loans charge prepayment fees if paid off early.
- When used strategically, a business loan can drive growth and improve financial stability.

There are many types of business loans, each designed to meet different needs. Below is an easy-to-follow guide to the most common loan options available in 2025.

### 1. Term Loans

Term loans offer a lump sum of money that you repay with interest over a fixed period. They come in three forms:

- **Short-term loans**: 3 to 18 months with higher interest rates.
- **Medium-term loans**: Typically repaid over 1 to 5 years.
- **Long-term loans**: Last between 3 and 25 years.

**Best for**: Large one-time expenses like purchasing inventory, equipment, or expanding operations.

### 2. SBA Loans

SBA loans are issued by banks or online lenders and partially guaranteed by the U.S. government. This makes them less risky for lenders and more accessible for borrowers.

- **SBA 7(a) Loans**: The most popular type—over 45,000 loans were approved in 2025, totaling nearly $20 billion.
- **SBA 504 Loans**: Best for buying real estate or large equipment, with terms up to 25 years and amounts up to $5 million.
- **SBA Express Loans**: Quicker approval with simpler paperwork.
- **SBA Microloans**: Loans under $50,000 are also available to some nonprofits, like childcare centers.

**Best for**: Startups, expansions, or refinancing debt with more favorable terms.

### 3. Business Lines of Credit

A business line of credit gives you flexible access to funds up to a set limit.

- Only pay interest on the money you use.
- The credit renews as you repay (revolving credit).
- Funds can be used for nearly any business purpose.
- Limits often start at $25,000 and may be secured by assets.

**Best for**: Managing cash flow, covering emergencies, or recurring short-term needs.

### 4. Equipment Financing

This loan helps you buy machinery, tools, or vehicles. The equipment itself serves as collateral.

- Loan amounts range from $500 to $5 million.
- Easier approval, even with a lower credit score (usually 600+).

**Best for**: Businesses needing expensive equipment without paying upfront.

### 5. Invoice Financing (or Factoring)

These options let you unlock cash tied up in unpaid invoices.

- **Invoice factoring**: Sell your invoices to a third party for immediate cash.
- **Invoice financing**: Use your invoices as collateral to borrow money while keeping control of collections.

**Best for**: B2B businesses with long payment cycles needing faster access to cash.

### 6. Merchant Cash Advances

A merchant cash advance gives you a lump sum upfront in exchange for a percentage of future credit card sales.

- Repayments happen daily or weekly.
- Charges are based on a “factor rate,” not traditional interest.
- Quick to access, but often more expensive in the long run.

**Best for**: Businesses with strong daily credit card sales but limited credit history.

### 7. Specialized Loans

Depending on your business goal, you may need one of these targeted loan types:

- **Commercial Real Estate Loans**: For buying land or buildings. Loans start at $25,000 with terms up to 15 years.
- **Business Acquisition Loans**: To buy an existing business.
- **International Trade Loans**: Backed by the SBA, these help small businesses involved in import/export.
- **Startup Loans**: Although harder to get, startups may qualify for small loans or equipment financing within 3–6 months of operation, depending on revenue and credit.

## Our Expert Tips to Reduce Business Loans

Taking out a business loan can be a smart way to fund growth, but paying more than necessary isn’t. Here are our expert strategies to help you **minimize borrowing costs** and **get the most value** from your loan:

- **Improve your credit score before applying:** A higher credit score helps you qualify for better interest rates and loan terms. Work on paying off existing debts, fixing any errors on your credit report, and making all payments on time.
- **Compare multiple lenders, not just interest rates:** Get quotes from banks, credit unions, and online lenders. Look beyond interest rates—check for fees, repayment flexibility, and customer service quality.
- **Borrow what you truly need:** Avoid over-borrowing. The more you borrow, the more interest you'll pay.
- **Choose the shortest repayment term:** Shorter loan terms mean higher monthly payments but lower total interest costs. If your cash flow allows, go for a shorter term to save more over time.
- **Avoid merchant cash advances:** MCAs are easy to access but extremely expensive. Use them only as a last resort when traditional loans are not available.
- **Build a strong, clear business plan:** Lenders prefer borrowers who demonstrate how the loan will generate a return on investment. A solid business plan can help you secure better terms and faster approvals.

## Bottom Line

Business loans can be a powerful tool to scale your business when used wisely. By understanding the loan process, comparing your options, and using tools like Avada’s free Business Loan Calculator, you can make more confident, data-driven financial decisions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the monthly payment on a $50,000 business loan?

The monthly payment depends on the **interest rate** and **loan term**. Here are some quick estimates:

| **Term** | **Interest Rate** | **Estimated Monthly Payment** |

| 3 years | 8% | \~$1,567 |
| 5 years | 8% | \~$1,013 |

### How much income do I need for a $500,000 business loan?

Lenders typically want your **annual business revenue to be at least 1.25x–1.5x** your annual loan payments. Here’s an estimate:

- **Example**: A 5-year loan at 8% = \~$10,138/month
- Recommended annual income = **$150,000–$200,000 minimum**, ideally higher with strong cash flow and credit history.

### Is it hard to get a $100,000 business loan?

**No**, getting a $100,000 business loan is achievable, especially if your business is in good financial shape. You’ll typically need a credit score of 650 or higher, at least $100,000 in annual revenue, and a business history of at least six months (for online lenders) or two years (for banks). While traditional banks offer lower interest rates, they have stricter requirements. Online lenders are faster and more flexible, but often come with higher rates.

### Can I get a $400,000 business loan?

**Yes**, it’s possible to get a $400,000 business loan, but it usually requires strong qualifications. Lenders will look for annual revenue of at least $500,000, a credit score of 680, and a business track record of at least one to two years. For larger loans, lenders may also ask for collateral, detailed financial documents, and a clear explanation of how you’ll use the funds.

### What is the typical interest rate for a business loan?

Interest rates vary based on the loan type, lender, credit profile, and business performance. On average:

- **Traditional bank loans** range from 4% to 10%
- **SBA loans** generally fall between 6% and 10%
- **Online lenders** may charge between 8% and 30%+
- **Merchant cash advances** often carry much higher effective rates.

### Will a business loan affect my ability to get a mortgage?

**Yes**, a business loan can impact your mortgage application, particularly if it’s personally guaranteed or affects your **debt-to-income ratio**. Mortgage lenders may also review your business obligations and require additional documentation if your income is tied to the business.

### Are business loans tax-deductible?

Yes, **business loans themselves are not tax-deductible**, but the **interest you pay on a business loan typically is**—as long as the loan is used for legitimate business purposes. This means if you borrow money to buy equipment, fund operations, or invest in growth, the **interest payments** can usually be deducted as a business expense on your taxes.

### Does a business loan affect personal credit?

It **can**, depending on how the loan is structured. If the loan is **personally guaranteed** or taken out in your name, missed payments or defaults can appear on your personal credit report. However, if the loan is strictly under your business’s name and EIN (Employer Identification Number), and not personally guaranteed, it usually doesn’t affect your personal credit—unless the business defaults.

### Should I get a business loan?

You **should consider** a business loan if:

- You need capital to grow or stabilize your business.
- You have a solid plan for using the funds (e.g. buying inventory, expanding, marketing).
- Your projected returns outweigh the cost of the loan.
- Avoid taking a loan if you’re unsure how you’ll repay it or if the business is already struggling with debt.

### Do business loans count as income?

**No,** business loans are not considered income for tax or accounting purposes. When a business receives loan funds, they are classified as a liability, not revenue, because the amount must be repaid. As a result, the loan does not appear as income on your profit and loss statement or business tax return.

### Are business loans worth it?

Yes, business loans can be worth it —they provide access to capital that can help grow your company, invest in equipment, hire staff, or cover cash flow gaps. However, their value depends on the loan’s terms, interest rates, your ability to repay, and whether the borrowed funds will generate a return greater than the cost of the loan.

## What Is the Profit Margin Formula?

The **profit margin formula** measures how much profit a business makes for every dollar of sales. There are different types of profit margins (gross, operating, and net), but the most commonly used is **net profit margin**.

This calculation provides valuable insight into your company's overall profitability and serves as a strategic guide for pricing decisions and long-term financial sustainability.

***Profit Margin = (Gross Profit/Net Revenue) x 100***

The formula helps businesses track financial health, compare performance across periods, and benchmark against competitors in their industry.

### *So, What Is a Good Profit Margin?*

A good profit margin can vary depending on the industry. This is because different types of businesses have unique cost structures and pricing power. For example, it wouldn’t make sense to compare the profit margins of a retail store with those of an oil and gas company—they work in different conditions.

That said, there are some general benchmarks businesses can use to measure performance:

- **Gross profit margin**: 20% to 40% is usually considered strong
- **Operating profit margin**: 10% to 20% is often healthy
- **Net profit margin**: 5% to 10% is solid, while anything over 10% is excellent

From firsthand experience, these ranges help businesses quickly assess how efficiently they’re operating. For example, during my time working with small eCommerce brands, a net margin of just 7–8% was seen as a good sign, especially after accounting for ads, shipping, and overhead costs.

To back this up with data, a 2024 study by [**New York University’s Stern School of Business**](https://revenue.ky.gov/News/Publications/Capitalization%20Rate%20Study/2024%20CAP%20Rate%20Study%20-%20TEXT_FINAL.pdf) showed that net profit margins across various sectors ranged from **29%** to **33%**. For example, **hotel and gaming businesses** reported an average net margin of **10.08%**, while **money center banks** reached as high as **30.89%**.

## Types of Profit Margins

Businesses use several types of profit margins to measure profitability at different operational levels. Each type provides unique insights into a company's financial performance:

### 1. Gross Profit Margin

The gross profit margin calculator measures the percentage of revenue that exceeds the cost of goods sold (COGS). This metric focuses on production efficiency.

**Formula**: (Revenue – COGS) / Revenue × 100%

For example, if a company has $100,000 in revenue and $60,000 in COGS, the gross profit margin is 40%.

### 2. Operating Profit Margin

The operating profit margin reveals the percentage of revenue remaining after accounting for both COGS and operating expenses. This margin helps assess operational efficiency by showing how well a company manages its day-to-day expenses.

**Formula**: Operating Profit / Revenue × 100%

**For example,** the retail clothing store has:

- **Revenue**: $500,000
- **Cost of Goods Sold**: $300,000
- **Operating Expenses (rent, salaries, utilities, etc.):** $150,000

**Calculation:**

- Operating Profit = $500,000 – $300,000 – $150,000 = $50,000
- Operating Profit Margin = ($50,000 ÷ $500,000) × 100% = 10%

**Interpretation:** The company retains 10% of its revenue after paying for direct product costs and day-to-day operational expenses.

### 3. Net Profit Margin

The net profit margin calculator represents the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses, such as operating costs, taxes, and interest. It is the most comprehensive profitability metric, showing the company's overall financial performance.

**Formula**: Net Profit / Revenue × 100%

**Example:** A software company analyzing one of its products:

- **Price per unit**: $200
- **Variable costs per unit (customer service, hosting):** $50

**Calculation:**

- Contribution Margin per Unit = $200 – $50 = $150
- Contribution Margin Ratio = ($150 ÷ $200) × 100% = 75%

**Interpretation:** Each unit sold contributes 75% of its revenue toward covering fixed costs and generating profit.

### 4. EBITDA Margin

The Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization (EBITDA) margin focuses on operational performance without the influence of financial and accounting decisions.

**Formula**: EBITDA / Revenue × 100%

### 5. Contribution Margin

The contribution margin calculates the profitability of individual products after accounting for variable costs.

**Formula**: (Revenue – Variable Costs) / Revenue × 100%

**Example:** A software company analyzing one of its products:

- **Price per unit**: $200
- **Variable costs per unit (customer service, hosting):** $50

**Calculation:**

- Contribution Margin per Unit = $200 – $50 = $150
- Contribution Margin Ratio = ($150 ÷ $200) × 100% = 75%

**Interpretation:** Each unit sold contributes 75% of its revenue toward covering fixed costs and generating profit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a 30% margin on $100?

A **30% margin on $100** means:

- $100 is the **selling price**
- Profit = 30% of $100 = **$30**
- Cost = $100 − $30 = **$70**

So, if you sell a product for $100 with a 30% margin, you're making $30 in profit.

### What is the formula for profit %?

The general formula to calculate **profit percentage** is: Profit% = (Profit / Cost Price) × 100%

- **Profit** = Selling Price − Cost Price. This tells you how much profit you make relative to your cost.

### Is a 33% profit margin good?

Yes, a **33% profit margin** is generally considered **very good**, particularly in retail, ecommerce, and service-based industries. It means you're keeping 33 cents of every dollar earned after covering all expenses. However, what's considered "good" still depends on your industry—some sectors, such as grocery or manufacturing, typically operate with much slimmer margins due to higher overhead or competitive pricing.

### Why profit margin is important?

Profit margin is significant because it shows how much money a business keeps after paying its costs. It tells whether the company is making a healthy profit or just breaking even. Moreover, profit margin helps owners and investors understand how efficiently the business is running. It guides important decisions like pricing, budgeting, and cost control. As a result, it becomes easier to plan for growth.

In addition, strong profit margins give a company a safety net during hard times. They also allow room to reinvest in marketing, new products, or better services.

### How do I calculate my profit margin?

To calculate your profit margin, follow these simple steps:

- **Step 1. Find your net profit:** Net Profit = Total Revenue – Total Expenses
- **Step 2. Use the profit margin formula:** Profit Margin (%) = (Net Profit ÷ Total Revenue) × 100

**For example:** If your business earns $10,000 in revenue and has $7,000 in expenses:

- Net Profit = $10,000 – $7,000 = $3,000
- Profit Margin = ($3,000 ÷ $10,000) × 100 = **30%**

### Does profit margin include taxes?

Yes, net profit margin includes taxes. It is calculated after deducting all expenses, including operating costs, interest, and taxes.

### Can profit margin be negative?

Yes, profit margin can be negative. This happens when a company's expenses are higher than its revenue, meaning it is operating at a loss.

### How to calculate profit margin formula?

To calculate profit margin, use this simple formula:

**Profit Margin (%) = (Net Profit ÷ Total Revenue) × 100**

- **Net Profit** is what remains after subtracting all expenses (including taxes, interest, and operating costs).
- **Total Revenue** is the total income from sales before any expenses are deducted.

**For example:** If your revenue is $50,000 and your total expenses are $35,000:

- Net Profit = $50,000 – $35,000 = $15,000

Profit Margin = ($15,000 ÷ $50,000) × 100 = **30%**

If you’re wondering *how to measure this effectively*, that’s where a **ROI calculator** comes in. **What is ROI calculator? ROI (Return on Investment)** is a key financial metric that evaluates how profitably an investment uses capital. It is the ratio between the net gain (profit) and the total cost of an investment. In simpler terms, ROI shows how much profit you earn for what you’ve spent, such as employee, inventory warehouse, ads, tools, or campaigns.

Here’s why ROI is important:

## How to Calculate ROI Formula?

Investors cannot accurately estimate the effectiveness of their investments without understanding how to calculate ROI. This is why the ROI formula serves as a fundamental tool in investment decisions.

The formula relies on two key components: the investment's gain and its cost. The basic ROI formula is: **ROI = (Net Profit / Total Investment) x 100%**

Or, written another way: **ROI = \[(Revenue – Cost) / Cost\] x 100%**

Where:

- **Revenue**: The total amount of money you earned from an activity or investment (e.g., total sales from an ad campaign
- **Total Investment:** The total amount of money you spent to run that activity (e.g., ad spend, tool subscription, staff costs).
- **Net Profit:** The difference between your revenue and your costs. Net Profit = Revenue – Cost.

To make this process easier, you can use a **return on investment ROI calculator**, which automatically computes your ROI percentage and helps you understand whether your investment is profitable or not.

This gives you the **return on investment as a percentage**, showing how much you earned (or lost) compared to what you spent.

- **If ROI > 0%**: You made a profit.
- **If ROI = 0%**: You broke even (no gain, no loss).
- **If ROI < 0%**: You lost money (the investment wasn’t profitable).

**For example,** if you invested **$10,000** in a marketing campaign that generated **$15,000** in sales.

- **Revenue (Total Return):** $15,000
- **Cost (Investment):** $10,000

Now apply the formula: {(15,000 – 10,000) / 10,000} x 100% = 50%

=> **ROI = 50%.** This means your investment returned 50% — for every dollar spent, you earned $1.50 in total revenue, which equals $0.50 in profit.

## What is the Difference between ROI, annualized ROI, and ROE?

Here’s a comparison table explaining the **difference between ROI, Annualized ROI, and ROE**:

| **Metric** | **Definition** | **Purpose** | **Fomula** | **Time Consideration** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ROI** (Return on Investment) | Measures the total return amount to the initial invested cost. | Evaluates the overall profitability of an investment. | ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Investment Cost) × 100 | No time factor. |
| **Annualized ROI** | Your average return per year. | Compares investments with different time periods. | Annualized ROI = \\(1 + ROI (decimal)\\)^(1/years) − 1 × 100 | **Includes time**, expressed per year. |
| **ROE** (Return on Equity) | Measures a company’s profitability relative to the shareholders’ equity invested. | Evaluates how efficiently a company uses its equity to generate profit. | ROE = (Net Income ÷ Shareholders’ Equity) × 100 | Typically measured **annually**. |

**The Verdict**:

- **ROI** tells you how much total return you earned.
- **Annualized ROI** shows how efficiently your investment grows *per year*.
- **ROE** focuses on profitability from the *shareholders’ perspective* rather than the total investment cost.

## Mistakes when Calculating ROI

While ROI is one of the simplest financial metrics, it’s also one of the most commonly **miscalculated**. Small errors in defining costs, time frames, or returns can lead to misleading conclusions and poor business decisions. Below are the most frequent mistakes to watch out for when using the business ROI calculator:

| # | **Common Mistake** | **Explanation** | **Impact** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Ignoring the Time Factor** | Reporting a single percentage without duration is misleading. For example, a 20% ROI in 3 months is very different from 20% in 3 years. | Leads to unfair comparisons between short- and long-term investments. |
| **2** | **Excluding Hidden or Indirect Costs** | Costs such as maintenance, training, transaction fees, and taxes are often overlooked. | Causes ROI to appear higher than reality and creates false optimism. |
| **3** | **Using Gross Revenue Instead of Net Profit** | ROI should be based on **net profit** (revenue minus all expenses), not total income. | Overstates profitability and distorts return. |
| **4** | **Mixing Currencies or Units** | When evaluating international projects, require exchange-rate and inflation adjustments. | Produces inconsistent ROI across regions or time periods. |
| **5** | **Failing to Adjust for Time Value of Money** | ROI doesn’t account for inflation or discounting. | Makes long-term returns seem better than they truly are. |
| **6** | **Comparing ROI Across Different Risk Levels** | Two investments with identical ROI may mask very different risk profiles. | May cause investors to favor high-risk options without realizing it. |
| **7** | **Rounding or Misstating Data** | Minor calculation errors, incorrect decimal placement, or rounding early can significantly alter results. | Reduces the accuracy and credibility of ROI analysis. |

## How to Actually Use Theme Detection (4 Proven Strategies)

Theme detection is not about choosing a theme. It’s about understanding **what role the theme actually plays in growth**.

### Strategy 1: Don't just detect one competitor's theme

Theme detection only works when you compare **many competitors** at once.

Analyzing a single store leads to weak conclusions. You don’t know whether the theme drives growth or is just a random choice. However, when you analyze multiple competitors, repeated patterns create real insight. Specifically, patterns allow you to:

- **Identify what likely affects results**: If many top stores use the same theme, it likely fits the niche’s buying behavior.
- **Avoid decisions based on exceptions**: If high-revenue stores use both free and paid themes, the theme is not the growth driver.
- **Understand the fundamental role of themes**: If premium themes only increase AOV, their impact is limited.
- **Reduce wasted time and budget**: Upgrading themes only works when data shows the theme is a constraint, not because the competitors use it.

#### What to do:

- **Step 1**: List 10 – 20 competitors in the same niche and price range
- **Step 2:** Detect the theme used by each store
- **Step 3:** Track the data in a spreadsheet with these columns:

- Theme name
- Theme type (free vs. paid)
- Number of products
- Primary category /niche
- Estimated revenue or traffic tier (if available)

As a result, theme detection becomes really competitive research, not guesswork.

#### What the data will show you:

Once you review all stores together, you can draw clear conclusions:

- If **most top competitors use the same premium theme**, it signals that the theme effectively supports conversion.
- If **successful stores use free themes**, paid themes are not required for growth.
- If **many stores use custom themes**, it suggests standard themes do not meet key functional needs.

#### Real-world example

We analyzed **50 fashion boutiques** generating approximately **$500K–$2M in annual revenue**.

**Theme distribution:**

- 62% used premium themes (Impulse or Prestige)
- 24% used Dawn (free)
- 14% used fully custom themes

**Key insight:**

Premium themes correlated with **better merchandising and upsell structure**, which lifted AOV without guaranteeing higher sales volume.

### Strategy 2: Don’t Assume Revenue Comes From the Theme

**Common mistake:** Seeing a high-revenue store using a premium theme and assuming the theme caused the growth.

**Correct mindset:** Theme detection helps you see **whether the theme supports conversion**, not whether it generates revenue.

**What to look for:**

- If premium themes correlate with higher AOV, design helps monetize traffic.
- If revenue leaders use mixed themes, design is not the growth driver.

**Key insight:** Theme detection helps you place design in the **right role**, not overestimate it.

### Strategy 3: Don’t Treat Theme Choice as a Design Decision

**Common mistake:** Choosing a theme based on looks or trends.

**Correct mindset:** Theme detection reveals **business and UX complexity**, not visual preference.

**What to look for:**

- Free themes indicate simple products and clear buying flows. Therefore, advanced functionality is not required.
- **Premium themes** signal the need for stronger merchandising. This includes improved product presentation, upsells, cross-sells, and structured navigation for collections.
- **Custom themes** point to non-standard requirements. In these cases, stores rely on unique buying flows, complex pricing logic, or product structures that exceed Shopify’s default capabilities.

**How to apply this insight:** If many competitors use custom themes, do not focus on aesthetics. Instead, identify which functional gaps in standard themes are missing in the niche.

### Strategy 4: Don’t Upgrade Your Theme Without a Clear Signal

This strategy helps you protect both time and budget.

**What theme detection prevents:** Many merchants upgrade themes because the site feels outdated, conversion drops, or competitors switch themes. However, in most cases, that is the wrong diagnosis.

**A simple validation check:** If top competitors perform well on free themes, the theme is unlikely the bottleneck. Instead, prioritize traffic quality, offer clarity, pricing strategy, and trust signals such as reviews and social proof.

**Key rule:** Upgrade your theme only when data clearly shows it is constraining performance. Otherwise, focus on higher-impact optimizations first.

Avada Shopify Theme Detector works on 95% of Shopify stores by scanning a store’s public source code, but there are a few cases where it fails. Below are the most common failure cases and why:

### Issue 2: Not a Shopify Store (wrong platform URL)

What happens: You may see **“Platform not supported”** error or no reliable theme result because the detector only works on the Shopify store.

If the site is WooCommerce/Wix/Webflow/BigCommerce, the Avada detector tool can’t find it.

**How to verify in 10 seconds:**

- Add **/admin** to the domain.
  - If it redirects to a Shopify admin login, it’s likely Shopify.

**Best solutions:**

| **Situation** | **What to do** |
| --- | --- |
| You’re unsure it’s Shopify | Use /admin check, or try another Shopify-specific check (e.g., storefront code hints). |
| It’s non-Shopify | Use a platform-specific detector (Woo/Wix) or treat it as a design reference only. |

### Issue 3: Headless/Custom Builds (15-20% of enterprise stores)

**What happens:** The detector returns something like “**Custom Theme**” or “**Cannot identify**”, even though the store might still be on Shopify.

### How can I find out the version of a Shopify theme?

There are three methods to check the version of a Shopify theme:
**Method 1: Check the theme version in your Shopify Admin**

- Step 1: Go to Shopify Admin > Online Store > Themes
- Step 2: Select the theme you want to check
- Step 3: Access the “…” (three-dot) option
- Step 4: Open Edit code or Customize
- Step 5: At the top of the theme editor, Shopify shows the exact theme name

**Method 2: Check via Free Avada Theme Detector with three steps**:

- Step 1: Insert the URL of the Shopify store
- Step 2: Scan the URL within 2 seconds

**Method 3: Check the version inside the theme files**

- Step 1: Go to Online Store > Themes > “…” (three-dot) > Edit code
- Step 2: Open config/settings_schema.json, or layout/theme.liquid
- Step 3: Look for fields such as "theme_version", "version” or a comment block with version info.

Choosing the right Shopify theme is crucial because it affects the store’s appearance, user experience, and engagement, directly influencing customer satisfaction and conversion rates.

### How to Choose Shopify Themes?

Choosing the right Shopify theme is crucial for creating a professional, user-friendly store that aligns with your brand, products, and content strategy. Here’s how to decide based on key factors.

- The Product: Choose a theme that aligns with the size and structure of your product catalog. Ensure product categories are clear and easy to navigate.
- The Content: Choose a theme that supports your content, such as photos, videos, and text. Avoid themes requiring elements you don’t have, like large images or specific overlays.
- The Support: Shopify themes come with dedicated support from Shopify’s team, while third-party themes rely on the developer’s availability. Always check reviews and confirm support options to ensure smooth troubleshooting if issues arise.

### How does the Shopify Theme Detector work?

The theme detector works by scanning the public source code of the Shopify website you enter. Most Shopify stores embed theme-related metadata in their code, either in theme.js or theme.css, or through identifiable tags in the section of the site.
**What we analyze**: 1. \`Shopify.theme\` JSON object (contains theme name and ID) 2. \`theme_store_id\` references (links to official Shopify themes) 3. Asset file naming patterns (e.g., theme-dawn-v1.2.css) 4. Section and snippet naming conventions **The matching process:**
We compare these identifiers with our database of 12,500+ known themes. Our algorithm cross-references multiple signals to ensure accuracy – a theme should match 3+ identifiers to confirm detection.

**What we return**: Theme name (e.g., "Impulse," "Dawn," "Prestige") Theme type (Official Shopify, Third-party marketplace, Custom-built) Theme ID (if available) Purchase link (if publicly available) Price (if applicable) **What we DON'T access:**

No login credentials required, no backend access needed, and no personal data collected. The detector analyzes only publicly accessible code, the same source code anyone can view by right-clicking and selecting “View Page Source.”

### Is the Shopify Theme Detector always accurate?

The answer is YES. A Shopify theme detector can be highly accurate, but it’s not 100% guaranteed.
When it’s usually accurate:

- The store uses popular Shopify themes
- Theme files and structure are unchanged
- The storefront is publicly accessible (not password-protected)

When it can be wrong or return “unknown:”

- The theme is heavily customized (files renamed, sections rebuilt)
- The store uses a custom theme (built in-house or by an agency)
- The theme is a clone of another theme
- The storefront is password-protected (limited public code to scan)

Yes, you can use the Avada Theme Detector on any publicly accessible Shopify store. The tool functions reliably regardless of the store’s size or geographic location. Simply ensure that the URL is correct and that the site is live (not password-protected or under maintenance).

The answer is YES. You can use a detected Shopify theme for your store, but only if you obtain it properly and respect the licensing rules.

# General Data Protection Regulation – GDPR
URL: https://avada.io/gdpr/
Markdown: https://avada.io/md/gdpr/

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides new, consistent standards across the EU to protect the rights of EU citizens regarding how their personal data is being used. It went into effect on May 25, 2018 and applies to any company that uses personal data from EU citizens.

We are committed to privacy and security and were ready for the GDPR as it came into effect on May 25, 2018. But that’s not all. As a Processor for your user data, we are also committed to making it easier for you to comply and equipping you, our customers, with easier paths towards your compliance with the GDPR

## GDPR Basics

Replacing the existing EU privacy directive 95/46/EC, which has been in place for over 20 years, the GDPR strengthens and expands the privacy rights of individuals in an era in which much of life takes place online.

The GDPR is extensive, affecting not just businesses based in the EU but also any company that processes the personal data of EU citizens. For instance, if you’re sending data about a person in the EU to AVADA, it’s likely that the GDPR applies to you.

The Data Protection Principles set forth in the GDPR include requirements like the following:

- Personal data collected must be processed in a fair, legal, and transparent way and should only be used in a way that a person would reasonably expect.
- Personal data should only be collected to fulfill a specific purpose and it should only be used for that purpose. Organizations must specify why they need the personal data when they collect it.
- Personal data should be held no longer than necessary to fulfill its purpose.
- People covered by the GDPR have the right to access their own personal data. They can also request a copy of their data, and that their data be updated, deleted, restricted, or moved to another organization.

We’d encourage you to read the text in full as well as to consult with your legal counsel for the most complete understanding of the GDPR.

## What Did AVADA do to Prepare for GDPR?

As a customer of AVADA who puts data about your end users into our product, you are a Data Controller. We act as a Data Processor for you. We’re also a Data Controller in supplying services to you (as a AVADA customer) and making decisions about your personal data.

We got ready for GDPR by preparing for our own compliance — as well as making it easy for you to comply as a data controller. Here is an overview of what we’ve done so far:

### Data Processing Agreement

We reviewed all our legal agreements and made any required changes to be GDPR compliant. We updated our [Data Processing Agreement](https://avada.io/md/dpa/), [Terms of Service](https://avada.io/md/tos/), and [Privacy Policy](https://avada.io/md/privacy-policy/) and posted them on our website in advance of the GDPR deadline. We also made sure that any vendors we use as sub-processors are GDPR compliant

### Security and Data Management

AVADA already employed strict policies and procedures around security and data management. Additionally, we designated an internal team and engaged outside expertise to enhance security standards that protect our customers’ data and follow GDPR requirements.

- We instituted processes that ensure prompt notifications to customers and GDPR authorities as required in the unlikely event of a data breach.
- We formalized and documented our internal policies related to data security.
- We put safeguards in place to ensure secure and proper handling of data stored outside of the EU as required.
- We will continue, as has been our practice, to only process personal data according to our customer’s instructions.

### Expanding Product Capabilities

To help you comply with Article 24 (responsibility of the controller) and your end users’ requests related to the right to access, data portability, right to erasure, right to object and the right to restrict processing — we enhanced AVADA with new product capabilities:

- Easy profile export: Export all data about a single profile in a simple standardized format to help you with requests from your end users regarding right to access and data portability.
- Automatic suppression: A new API endpoint that allows us to block any associated incoming personal data to help you comply with requests regarding the right to object or restrict.
- Audit trail: AVADA has provided limited auditing information upon request to date. We expanded and enhanced this capability by adding full audit trails for all changes to your AVADA account.

### Existing Product Capabilities

AVADA already enables compliance with requirements regarding the right of data rectification and the right to be forgotten:

- Right to rectify user data: GDPR gives individuals the right to rectify any inaccurate or incomplete personal data. In AVADA, data can be adjusted at any time with a simple identify call. This will create or update the associated profile with the newly provided data.
- Right to be forgotten: We make it easy for you to honor delete requests from your end users by calling the DELETE API, or using the UI to delete a profile. We ensure that any associated user data and historical data are quickly and permanently deleted from our data stores.
- Accountability: AVADA has role-based permissions, supports encryption at rest of all associated account data, and many data management tools.

We fully support the GDPR and think it’s a good thing to treat customers and their data with care and respect. Our mission is to help companies like yours create better customer experiences with relevant communication and that requires the fair and secure use of personal data that was given with full consent and transparency.

If you have any questions or concerns regarding GDPR and AVADA, please send us a detailed message to [support@avada.io](mailto:support@avada.io).

We begin by thoroughly examining the service’s core features, capabilities, and target users. This allows us to understand the underlying value proposition and the problem that the service aims to solve.

### 2. Real-Time Experience

To provide firsthand information, our team uses the service itself.

- In the case of POS systems, we explore transaction processing, inventory management, customer data management, and other functionalities.
- We examine installation, customization options, and overall usability for Shopify apps and themes.

### 3. Feature Examination

We delve deep into the service’s features, assessing their usefulness, functionality, and the value they bring to the user. Whether it’s a POS’s integration capabilities or a theme’s design flexibility, each feature is tested rigorously.

### 4. Customer Support Analysis

We evaluate the quality of customer support by posing as real customers. We gauge response times, the accuracy of replies, and the overall willingness of the support team to help.

### 5. Cost Assessment

We critically assess the pricing structure to ensure the service offers value for money. This involves comparing the price with the service’s features and against similar services in the market.

### 6. User Reviews and Feedback

We believe that a holistic review should consider the experiences of many users. As such, we examine user reviews and feedback across various platforms to understand expected trends, issues, and praise associated with the service.

### 7. Future Prospect Evaluation

Given the dynamic nature of e-commerce, it is crucial to choose services that evolve with time. We assess the service’s update history and any potential for future improvements or enhancements.

### 8. Compatibility and Integration

We check how well the service integrates with other Shopify services and any relevant third-party software. For instance, how seamlessly a POS system syncs with Shopify’s inventory management system or how well a theme plays with different Shopify apps.

### 9. Conclusive Summary

We conclude our review with a comprehensive summary that weighs the pros and cons. This allows our readers to understand the service’s overall value, suitability for different use cases, and whether it meets their specific requirements.

This meticulous, user-focused approach allows us to provide reliable, informative, and balanced reviews, helping our readers make informed decisions that benefit their businesses.

## Our Review Process

Here is the step-by-step process we follow when conducting reviews of point-of-sale systems, Shopify apps, Shopify themes, or any other service.

### Step 1: Initial Research

Our team begins with extensive research on the service we’re reviewing. This involves understanding its features, purpose, target users, pricing structure, and how it compares with similar services in the market.

### Step 2: Service Trial

We then sign up for or purchase the service to use it firsthand. We test every aspect of it, using all the features as a regular user would, and take note of the user interface, ease of use, and overall functionality.

### Step 3: Feature Testing

We delve deeper into each feature the service offers, evaluating its performance and how well it serves its purpose. For example, when reviewing a Shopify theme, we’d look at design flexibility, mobile responsiveness, SEO features, loading speed, etc.

### Step 4: Customer Support Evaluation

Next, we contact the service’s customer support with questions and requests, assessing their response time, helpfulness, and overall quality of service.

### Step 5: Pricing Analysis

We examine the service’s pricing structure, compare it with similar services in the market, and assess whether it offers good value for money.

### Step 6: User Reviews

We then go through user reviews on various platforms to gather feedback from other users. This helps us identify common issues or praises we may not have noticed during our usage.

### Step 7: Updates & Future Prospects

We also consider the service’s updated history and the company’s plans for its future development. This helps us assess whether the service will likely stay relevant and continue improving.

### Step 8: Integration Testing

Especially for software services, we test how well the service integrates with other relevant systems and tools, checking for any compatibility issues.

### Step 9: Drafting the Review

After gathering all this information, we draft our review, presenting our findings in a detailed, organized manner. We provide a balanced view, highlighting the service’s strengths and weaknesses.

### Step 10: Review Editing and Publication

Our editors then proofread and edit the review, ensuring it’s accurate and easy to understand. Once it meets our standards, we publish the review on our blog.

This detailed, hands-on review process helps us provide thorough and unbiased reviews to our readers.
